The Preply English-Tutor Market: ML Deep Dive

Clustering & classification with scikit-learn
8,952 unique tutors · 161 countries · collected 1–2 September 2026 · prices in USD per 50-minute lesson

Preply is an online tutoring marketplace that connects students with independent tutors for one-on-one video lessons; English is by far its largest category, with tens of thousands of tutors competing worldwide. Every tutor sets their own price and is sold through a listing card showing a handful of public signals: price per lesson, country of origin, star rating, review count, active students, lifetime lessons taught, a “native speaker” label, and platform badges such as Super Tutor. Students pick from ranked search results, and the platform takes a commission on every lesson — so those few card signals effectively decide who gets hired and at what price.

This report takes 8,952 of those listing cards for English tutors and asks what machine learning can extract from them: which tutor archetypes actually exist (clustering), and which signals predict a premium price or a full roster (classification).

Before any narrative, the scorecard. Two Random Forests were trained on three quarters of the data and tested on the quarter they never saw. One predicts whether a tutor charges a top-quartile price (≥$25) without seeing the price; the other predicts whether a tutor holds a top-quartile roster (≥19 active students) from card signals alone. Both beat chance comfortably — and both err in the same telling direction: they are cautious, missing real premiums and full rosters more often than they invent fake ones.

Executive summary. Averages and cross-tabs describe this market; here the algorithms draw the map instead. Four findings survive cross-validation:
  • The market has five archetypes, and one of them owns it. KMeans finds a five-cluster structure; the top cluster — established natives, 29% of tutors — captures 69% of the lifetime revenue proxy. The bottom two (newcomers plus a 45-tutor “reputation graveyard”) hold 23% of tutors and 0.3% of revenue.
  • The native premium is really a country premium. A Random Forest predicts top-quartile pricing with AUC 0.82, and almost all of that skill comes from one feature: the tutor’s country price level. Once the model knows it, the native-speaker flag adds nothing (permutation importance ≈ 0).
  • Prices are predictable; demand is not. The same model family predicting who has a full roster only reaches AUC 0.69 from card signals. The platform’s price structure is rigid; success within it is far more open.
  • Expensive tutors are fuller, not emptier. Among reviewed tutors, 41% of those charging over 3× their country’s median have a top-quartile roster, versus 23% of those below the median — and the model says price itself carries no independent signal. Price doesn’t buy demand; quality raises both.

1 · Method in one minute

A single September 2026 snapshot of public listing pages: 8,991 tutors with a usable price after de-duplication. Missing review/student/lesson counts are treated as zero (the card shows nothing when there is nothing); missing ratings are median-filled for clustering only. Seven features per tutor, all standardized: log price, rating, log reviews, log active students, log lifetime lessons, log lessons-per-student (the retention proxy), and the native-speaker flag.

  • Clustering: KMeans (k chosen by silhouette, see below), visualized through a 2-component PCA.
  • Classification: Random Forests (400 trees, 5-fold stratified cross-validation) on two targets: top-quartile price (≥$25) and top-quartile active students (≥19). Importance is measured by permutation — how much held-out AUC drops when a feature is shuffled — which, unlike impurity importance, does not reward a feature for merely being high-cardinality.
  • Leakage control: the demand model gets only what a student sees on the card before choosing (price, rating, flags) — review and lesson counts are excluded because they are consequences of demand, not predictors of it.

2 · Five archetypes, one winner

The silhouette score technically peaks at k = 3, but it is nearly flat through k = 5, and the three-cluster solution just rediscovers “newcomers, non-natives, natives.” At k = 5 the established pool splits into economically distinct tiers, so that is the segmentation reported here.

Projected onto two principal components, the market is a career conveyor belt. PC1 (51% of variance) is the track-record axis — reviews, students, lessons, and retention all load on it together. PC2 is the reputation axis, dominated by rating. Tutors enter on the left, move right as they accumulate history… and a tiny group falls off the bottom.

Three things the clusters say that the averages didn’t.
  • Natives get a ladder; non-natives get a wall. Natives split cleanly into a “climbing” tier (C2, 198 median lessons) and an incumbent tier (C4, 2,021). Non-natives have no intermediate cluster: they appear either as newcomers or as fully established professionals (C3) — consistent with a survival filter where non-natives who don’t reach escape velocity exit instead of lingering mid-ladder.
  • The graveyard is tiny because failure is fatal. C0 is just 45 tutors, and every one is rated ≤3.8 in a market whose median rating is 5.0. A visibly bad rating is so rare — and so terminal — that the algorithm isolates it as its own cluster: you don’t stay in this market with 3 stars, you leave it.
  • Half the market is economically invisible. C0 + C1 + C2 together are 42% of tutors and under 3% of the lifetime revenue proxy (price × lessons). The “market” the money sees is essentially C3 and C4.

3 · What predicts a premium price

Can a model spot a top-quartile price (≥$25) without seeing the price? Yes — cross-validated AUC 0.82 ± 0.01 — but the skill is astonishingly concentrated. Shuffle the tutor’s country price level (the median price of their country) and AUC collapses by 0.23. Shuffle anything else and it barely moves. Track record (retention, lifetime lessons) comes a distant second; ratings, reviews, and badges are rounding errors.

The passport premium is a country premium. On its own, the native-speaker flag looks decisive — natives charge far more. The model sharpens that: conditional on country price level, the native flag’s permutation importance is zero (−0.003). “Native” pays only through which passport it correlates with — a US native and a US non-native price alike; a US native and a Philippine native do not.

How simple can the pricing rule get? A depth-3 decision tree — three questions — reaches AUC 0.80, almost matching the 400-tree forest:

Reading the right-hand path: country median ≥ $19 → roughly 300+ lifetime lessons → rating above 4.8 — and the premium probability hits 60%, double the 30% base rate. That is the entire premium formula: an expensive passport, a long history, a spotless rating. In that order.

4 · What predicts a full roster

Flip the question: among the 7,586 tutors with at least one review, who holds a top-quartile roster (≥19 active students)? Given only what a student sees on the card before choosing — price, rating, native flag, badge, country — the model reaches just AUC 0.69.

That gap is the finding. The market prices tutors by a rigid, almost mechanical formula (AUC 0.82 from one feature), but it does not allocate students by one. Demand runs on things the card can’t fully see — subject fit, availability, video quality, word of mouth.

Of the visible signals, rating matters most (importance 0.09), then the native flag (0.04) and the Super Tutor badge (0.02). And price? Slightly negative importance — shuffling it doesn’t hurt the model at all. Yet the raw curve on the right rises monotonically: tutors at >3× their country median are full 41% of the time, versus 23% for everyone at or below the median.

Expensive tutors are fuller — but not because of the price. Put both facts together: demand rises with relative price in the raw data, while price carries no independent signal once rating, nativeness, and badges are known. The demand curve is quality (and survivorship) showing through price, not price creating demand. For tutors, the practical read: a justified raise doesn’t scare off a market that is already full at 3× the median. For learners: a high price predicts popularity, not availability of anything the card doesn’t already tell you.

5 · What the models add to the averages

The averages sayThe models add
Country explains 41% of price variance; the native flag another big chunk. One engineered feature — country price level — carries essentially all model skill (AUC 0.82); the native flag is redundant once country is known.
Revenue is concentrated: top decile of tutors takes half the market. Concentration has a shape: it is one specific archetype (29% of tutors, native, 2,000+ lessons) taking 69%, while 42% of tutors share 3%.
Expensive tutors keep students longer (retention by price band). The full demand curve is monotone in relative price — and a leakage-controlled model shows the price itself carries no independent demand signal.
The Super Tutor badge correlates with retention; “Professional” is decoration. Confirmed under permutation: Super Tutor is the 3rd demand signal (0.02) and a rounding error for price (0.008).
Market has arrival cohorts and a long tail. The tail has structure: a career conveyor (PC1 = track record), a ladder natives climb in two steps, a wall non-natives either clear or exit at — and a 45-tutor graveyard proving that bad ratings end careers.

6 · Limitations

  • Everything is correlational. “Price carries no independent demand signal” means no signal given these features in this snapshot — not that a tutor can raise prices consequence-free.
  • Country price level is computed from this same dataset (median of ~8,991 tutors), so each tutor contributes a sliver to their own feature. With 50+ tutors in every major country the leak is negligible, but AUC 0.82 should be read as “association strength,” not deployable forecasting skill.
  • The silhouette score is nearly flat between k = 3 and 5; the five-cluster story is a defensible resolution choice, not a unique optimum. Cluster boundaries (especially C2/C3) are soft.
  • students counts active students against lifetime lessons, so lessons-per-student overstates absolute retention (comparisons between clusters remain valid).
  • Single snapshot; the “conveyor belt” reading of PC1 is a cross-sectional inference, not observed motion. Coverage is the union of 8 locale ranking windows, so long-tail non-natives are under-sampled.
